questions.prompt: Which source type most commonly breaks a merged timeline?
options: Windows event logs, which use UTC internally
Application logs recorded in local time with no offset, which merge into a UTC timeline displaced by hours
Cloud audit logs, which have no timestamps
questions.explanation: A displaced event does not look wrong -- it looks like a different event, which is what makes unconverted local-time sources so dangerous in a merged timeline.

questions.prompt: How is host clock skew calibrated?
options: By comparing the host clock to an internet time server after the fact
By finding one event recorded independently in two places -- such as a logon in both the workstation and domain controller logs -- and computing the difference
By assuming a standard one-hour offset
questions.explanation: With one authoritative source and one measured against it, the difference gives a constant offset that re-aligns every other timestamp from the skewed host.

questions.prompt: Why is reading a super-timeline start to finish not a viable technique?
options: Timeline tools do not support sequential reading
A full-disk super-timeline runs to millions of rows -- the method is to pivot from a known event and expand outward
Timelines are stored in random order
Only the first thousand rows are accurate
questions.explanation: Pivoting from the alert, the ransom note creation, or the first detection and filtering tightly around it is what makes the volume tractable.

questions.prompt: When a timeline built from $SI timestamps looks implausible, what are the corroborating sources?
options: $FN timestamps and the USN journal, which record events rather than state and are generally not scrubbed by timestomping tools
questions.explanation: Timestomping targets $SI, which is what most timeline tools read by default -- so the kernel-maintained $FN and the append-only journal provide the independent check.
